origin: American Red Cross and NIH MedlinePlus; new manuscript

action.text: Stop all activity immediately, seat or lay the person comfortably at rest in shelter, and log the exact minute symptoms started (critical for hospital stroke treatment windows).

Check stroke signs rapidly—Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness or drift, Speech slurred or strange—and treat chest pressure, sweating, nausea, or sudden unexplained collapse as urgent cardiac/medical emergencies.

Call 911 immediately and follow dispatcher instructions; do NOT let the patient drive, walk out strenuously, or take unprescribed medications unless a 911 dispatcher or clinician specifically directs it.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Treat sudden cardiac or stroke warning signs as time-critical emergencies rather than hiking fatigue.
applies: Adults experiencing unexplained chest pressure, jaw/arm pain, shortness of breath, sudden facial droop, arm weakness, or slurred speech.
equipment: Communication device, insulating ground pad, shade/shelter, and written symptom-onset time log.

failure.text: Assuming chest tightness or slurred speech is just dehydration and having the person hike back to the trailhead.

verify.text: Confirm exact symptom-onset time is written down, exertion has stopped, and emergency transport is inbound.

stop.text: Any loss of consciousness or abnormal breathing transitions immediately to 911 dispatcher-guided CPR and AED retrieval.

diagram: Spot chest pain or FAST stroke signs | Stop exertion & log exact onset time | Call 911; follow dispatcher guidance
visual: Four-step acute cardiac and stroke response plate covering recognition, exact onset logging, rest/shelter, and 911 activation. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Decide between walk-out, assisted exit, and staying put for SAR extraction
origin: NPS Emergency Plan and NIH MedlinePlus; new manuscript

action.text: Consider walking out ONLY when the patient is fully alert, stable across repeated checks, able to bear weight safely without worsening the injury, and daylight/weather allow a conservative exit.

Stay put, shelter, insulate, and call organized SAR whenever the patient has severe bleeding, shock, altered mental status, head/spine/pelvis/femur injury, heat stroke, severe hypothermia, or cannot walk safely.
Weigh nightfall, steep slippery terrain, and rescuer exhaustion honestly—two exhausted companions trying to drag an injured hiker down steep trails frequently trigger secondary falls.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Match evacuation strategy to patient stability, terrain difficulty, daylight, and party capacity without creating new casualties.
applies: Any backcountry injury or illness where the party must choose whether to self-evacuate or summon organized rescue.
equipment: Map, trip plan, daylight/weather forecast, communication device, and written patient trend log.

failure.text: Attempting an improvised late-afternoon carryout over wet roots with an unstable patient instead of establishing warm shelter and calling SAR early.

verify.text: Confirm all party members agree on the evacuation threshold, shelter capacity, water/warmth reserves, and who maintains communication.

stop.text: Any deterioration in patient stability, darkness, storm onset, or rescuer fatigue halts movement immediately in favor of warm shelter and SAR activation.

diagram: Stable & walks safely -> controlled exit | Red flags / unstable -> stay & call SAR | Stop movement if party tires or darkens
visual: Decision tree evaluating patient red flags, walking stability, and terrain/daylight limits to select self-exit versus organized SAR. Conceptual, not to scale.
reviewer: Search and rescue and wilderness medicine

title: Recognize improvised litter hazards and when not to move a patient
origin: NPS Emergency Plan and NIH MedlinePlus; new manuscript

action.text: Do NOT move a non-ambulatory patient with suspected neck, spine, pelvis, femur, or internal injury unless immediate life-threatening scene danger (rising floodwater, fire, rockfall, or airway threat) forces a short urgent move.

Recognize that improvised pole-and-jacket litters require six to eight fresh rotating carriers on uneven trails and often collapse, drop the patient, or exhaust small parties within a few hundred yards.
Prioritize building warm windproof ground-insulated shelter around the patient in place while activating professional SAR litter teams equipped with rigid stretchers and rigging.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent catastrophic secondary spinal, bleeding, or drop injuries caused by premature improvised carries.
applies: Non-ambulatory injured persons in backcountry terrain before trained SAR litter teams arrive.
equipment: Insulating pads, shelter tarp/tent, dry layers, and communication device.

failure.text: Loading a suspected spinal-injury patient onto a sagging improvised jacket stretcher with three tired hikers on a rocky descent.

verify.text: Confirm scene is stable, patient is insulated in place, and SAR dispatch knows the patient is non-ambulatory and requires a litter team.

stop.text: If a life-threatening hazard forces moving an injured person, keep the body aligned as one unit over the shortest distance to safety, then halt and stabilize.

diagram: No imminent danger -> shelter in place | Improvised carries risk drops/spine harm | Request trained SAR litter team
visual: Correct versus incorrect non-ambulatory management contrasting in-place thermal shelter and SAR litter activation against fragile under-staffed improvised carries. Conceptual, not to scale.
reviewer: Search and rescue and trauma EMS

title: Coordinate air-ambulance medical rescue under strict crew exclusion rules
origin: NPS Visitor Protection Aviation Program; new manuscript

action.text: Clear or weigh down all loose tarps, sleeping pads, hats, and plastic bags well before the aircraft approaches—rotor wash hurls loose gear into tail rotors and faces at high speed.

Shield the patient's eyes and airway from blowing dust, gravel, or snow, stay seated/crouched well clear of the landing area, and keep all bystanders completely back until the flight crew explicitly signals you.
Never approach a helicopter from behind (tail rotor), uphill side, or on your own initiative; follow explicit hand signals or radio instructions from the crew or dispatch exclusively.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Keep patients, bystanders, and loose gear completely clear of rotor-wash hazards while flight crews control every air-rescue step.
applies: Remote medical emergencies where dispatch notifies the party that a rescue helicopter is inbound.
equipment: Secure packs/tarps, eye protection if carried, high-contrast clothing kept weighed down, and active comms with dispatch.

failure.text: Running excitedly toward a landing rescue helicopter with an unsecured tarp fluttering beside the patient.

verify.text: Confirm all loose equipment is secured inside closed packs, bystanders are accounted for well clear, and one person relays dispatch prompts.

stop.text: Any unsecured debris, shifting bystanders, or unclear crew signal requires holding completely still in place until crew personnel walk to you.

diagram: Secure all loose gear early | Shield patient & hold well clear | Wait for explicit flight-crew direction
visual: System separation schematic showing helicopter rotor-wash exclusion perimeter, secured gear zone, and crew-controlled approach gate. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Sustain overnight remote patient stabilization during delayed rescue
origin: NWS Winter Shelter and NIH MedlinePlus; new manuscript

action.text: Place maximum ground insulation beneath an immobile patient first—an injured person generates minimal body heat and loses warmth rapidly into cold soil or snow even in mild seasons.

Protect the patient's shelter from wind and rain, maintain scheduled mental-status and breathing checks through the night, and keep caregivers fed, hydrated, and rotating rest shifts so no one collapses from exhaustion.
Offer small sips of safe potable water ONLY if the patient is fully alert, swallowing normally, and has no suspected shock, abdominal injury, or imminent surgery red flags.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Protect an immobilized patient from hypothermia, pressure sores, and dehydration when extraction takes many hours.
applies: Any immobilized or ill backcountry patient awaiting next-day or weather-delayed SAR evacuation.
equipment: Thick ground insulation, dry sleeping bags, windproof shelter, headlamp, warm/safe fluids (if alert and allowed), and monitoring log.

failure.text: Giving all sleeping pads to caregivers while the injured patient lies on a thin raincoat overnight and slips into hypothermia before dawn.

verify.text: Confirm ground insulation, dry outer barrier, scheduled caregiver watch shifts, and ongoing timed patient notes are active.

stop.text: Rapid deterioration in warmth, alertness, or breathing overnight triggers immediate re-contact with dispatch/beacon activation if not already deployed.

diagram: Max insulation under immobile patient | Rotate caregiver watch & log trends | Offer safe sips only if alert & no shock
visual: Overnight stabilization timeline mapping dusk insulation setup, scheduled watch rotations, hydration/airway checks, and dawn SAR handoff. Conceptual, not to scale.
reviewer: Wilderness medicine and search and rescue

title: Control junctional bleeding where a tourniquet cannot be placed
origin: ACS STOP THE BLEED; new manuscript

action.text: Call 911 immediately and expose the junctional wound completely so pressure lands straight on the bleeding vessel rather than surrounding tissue.

Apply firm, continuous, uninterrupted direct pressure straight into the bleeding source; responders trained in Stop the Bleed may pack clean or hemostatic gauze tightly into deep groin/armpit cavities (NEVER pack the neck, chest, or abdomen) and hold continuous pressure.
Keep the patient warm and insulated against shock while maintaining steady downward pressure without releasing to check until EMS assumes control.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize life-threatening groin, armpit, or neck bleeding and maintain continuous targeted pressure until EMS arrives.
applies: Severe bleeding in junctional zones (neck, shoulder/armpit, groin/hip) where extremity tourniquets cannot physically encircle the limb.
equipment: Clean sterile gauze (or hemostatic gauze if carried and trained), gloves, and continuous two-handed direct pressure.

failure.text: Trying to wrap an extremity tourniquet loosely around a hip or neck, or packing gauze into a chest or abdominal stab wound.

verify.text: Confirm steady uninterrupted pressure directly on the bleeding point, zero packing of neck/chest/abdomen, and active EMS response.

stop.text: Never release effective pressure prematurely; if caregiver hands fatigue, swap hands smoothly with a second responder while keeping constant downward force.

diagram: Tourniquet cannot fit groin/armpit/neck | Hold firm uninterrupted direct pressure | Pack deep groin/armpit only if trained
visual: Conceptual anatomical orientation schematic distinguishing extremity tourniquet zones from junctional direct-pressure/packing boundaries and non-packable torso cavities. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Manage routine nosebleeds while spotting head-trauma or severe hemorrhage flags
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Bleeding; new manuscript

action.text: Have an alert person sit upright leaning slightly forward (NOT backward) so blood drains forward instead of down the throat, which triggers coughing, vomiting, and airway irritation.
Pinch the soft lower portion of the nose firmly below the bony bridge continuously for 10 full minutes without peeking, breathing calmly through the mouth.

Escalate immediately to emergency care if bleeding follows a significant head/face impact, includes clear watery fluid mixed with blood, continues beyond 20 minutes of firm pinching, or causes dizziness/weakness.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Stop uncomplicated nosebleeds cleanly while recognizing when nasal bleeding signals serious trauma or uncontrolled blood loss.
applies: Spontaneous dry-air/altitude nosebleeds versus post-impact facial or head-injury bleeding.
equipment: Clean tissues or gauze, watch, and cool compress if available.

failure.text: Tilting the patient's head backward and pinching only the hard upper bony bridge while blood runs down their throat.

verify.text: Confirm upright forward lean, steady 10-minute lower-soft-nose pinch, and absence of head-injury or dizziness red flags.

stop.text: Heavy persistent bleeding, blood-thinning medication with uncontrolled flow, breathing difficulty, or dizziness requires urgent clinical evaluation.

diagram: Sit upright & lean slightly forward | Pinch soft lower nose 10 min steady | Escalate for trauma, >20 min or dizziness
visual: Correct versus incorrect nosebleed positioning contrasting upright forward-leaning soft-nose pinch against hazardous head-back posture. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Spot suspected internal bleeding and prioritize urgent EMS evacuation
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Bleeding and Shock; new manuscript

action.text: Suspect internal bleeding after hard torso/pelvis/thigh impacts or when a person shows rigid tender abdomen, expanding bruising, coughing or vomiting blood, dark tarry/bloody stool, or worsening dizziness/pallor.
Activate 911 immediately—internal hemorrhage cannot be stopped by field dressings and requires rapid hospital surgical stabilization.
Keep the patient completely still, horizontal and insulated from cold ground, withhold all food and fluids (NPO), and monitor alertness and breathing continuously.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize hidden internal hemorrhage after blunt trauma or illness where no external wound is visible.
applies: High-force falls, bicycle/ATV/snowmobile crashes, struck-by-log blows, or sudden severe abdominal pain/collapse.
equipment: Ground insulation, blankets, written monitoring log, and emergency communications.

failure.text: Dismissing a hard handlebar blow to the belly as "just getting the wind knocked out" and letting the person hike on as shock develops silently.

verify.text: Confirm mechanism of injury, abdominal/bruising signs, vital trends, and urgent evacuation request are documented clearly.

stop.text: Any signs of progressive shock (pale clammy skin, fast weak pulse, confusion) mandate highest-priority emergency extraction.

diagram: Blunt torso blow or blood vomit/cough | Keep still, insulated & strictly NPO | Expedite urgent hospital surgical care
visual: Failure-mode diagram tracing silent blunt-trauma internal hemorrhage through shock cues to immediate NPO stabilization and EMS transport. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Clean minor cuts and abrasions with potable water and protect against dirt
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Wounds and CDC Safe Water; new manuscript

action.text: Wash your own hands (or wear clean gloves) first, then rinse the minor wound thoroughly under steady clean potable water to flush out dirt, grit, and surface debris.

Wash surrounding intact skin gently with mild soap and safe water, avoiding pouring harsh alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, or full-strength iodine directly inside open tissue where they irritate healing cells.
Pat surrounding skin dry with clean gauze, cover the wound completely with a clean sterile dressing, and re-check daily for moisture, dirt breakthrough, or infection signs.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Reduce field wound infection risk using clean potable-water irrigation and protective dressings without damaging healthy tissue.
applies: Superficial minor cuts, scrapes, and abrasions after bleeding is controlled.
equipment: Confirmed potable drinking water (or sterile saline), clean syringe/bag for gentle flushing, mild soap for surrounding intact skin, and sterile non-stick dressings.

failure.text: Rinsing an open scrape in untreated creek water or sealing muddy grit inside a wound with tight tape.

verify.text: Confirm only confirmed potable/boiled-and-cooled water touched the wound, visible grit is flushed out, and the dressing stays clean and dry.

stop.text: Deep gaping cuts, heavy dirt that will not flush clean, hand/face/joint wounds, or unknown tetanus status require prompt clinical care.

diagram: Clean hands & flush with potable water | Avoid harsh chemicals inside open wound | Cover clean; inspect daily for infection
visual: Four-step minor wound-care plate showing hand hygiene, potable-water irrigation, surrounding skin cleaning, and sterile covering. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Stabilize impaled objects in place and escalate deep puncture wounds
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Wounds; new manuscript

action.text: If an object is impaled deeply in the body, do NOT pull it out—the object may be plugging a severed blood vessel, and removing it can trigger fatal internal or external hemorrhage.
Control bleeding around the base with gentle pressure on either side without pressing on the object itself, build bulky donut-style padding around it to prevent movement, and activate 911/EMS.

Treat all deep puncture wounds (even small ones that barely bleed, such as stepping on a rusty nail or deep stick puncture) as high-infection and tetanus hazards requiring clinical cleaning and evaluation.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent catastrophic bleeding and deep tissue damage by never pulling out impaled objects and recognizing hidden puncture infection risks.
applies: Branches, glass, metal, arrows, or fishhooks deeply embedded in tissue, plus deep nail/thorn/splinter punctures.
equipment: Bulky clean gauze pads, roller bandage/tape, and emergency communication.

failure.text: Pulling a wooden branch out of a thigh or chest in the backcountry and triggering massive uncontrollable arterial bleeding.

verify.text: Confirm impaled object is padded immobile without shifting, surrounding bleeding is monitored, and clinical evacuation is underway.

stop.text: Any impaled object in the head, neck, eye, chest, or abdomen is an immediate life-threatening emergency requiring urgent EMS extraction.

diagram: Never pull deeply impaled objects | Build bulky stabilizing pad around base | Expedite EMS; clinically review punctures
visual: Correct versus incorrect impaled-object care contrasting bulky base-padding stabilization against hazardous field removal. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Understand why lay responders do not suture or glue dirty backcountry wounds
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Wounds; new manuscript

action.text: Irrigate accessible superficial lacerations thoroughly with clean potable water, approximate edges only lightly with clean dressings if needed for bleeding control, and arrange clinical evaluation within standard medical windows.

Never stitch wounds with improvised sewing needles, staple skin, or seal dirty, jagged, puncture, or animal-bite wounds shut with household superglue—trapping bacteria inside an airtight wound causes severe deep abscess and sepsis.
Keep the wound moist-clean under sterile gauze protected from dirt, elevate an injured limb if comfortable, and monitor closely for infection during exit.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent trapped deep bacterial infections by leaving wound closure to clinical settings and using clean covered dressings in the field.
applies: Gaping lacerations, bite wounds, or contaminated cuts occurring hours away from a clinic.
equipment: Potable irrigation water, sterile gauze dressings, and rolled bandage.

failure.text: Sealing a muddy trail laceration or dog bite shut with cyanoacrylate glue in camp, trapping anaerobic bacteria deep beneath the skin.

verify.text: Confirm wound was irrigated with potable water, covered cleanly without improvised closure, and scheduled for prompt clinical review.

stop.text: Gaping wounds, exposed fat/tendon/bone, heavy contamination, facial cuts, or bite wounds require timely professional medical closure and tetanus/antibiotic review.

diagram: Irrigate cleanly with potable water | Never suture or superglue dirty wounds | Cover sterile & evacuate for clinical care
visual: System boundary diagram contrasting open sterile-dressed field protection against sealed-in bacterial contamination from improvised closure. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Recognize worsening wound infection and sepsis warning signs
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Wounds; new manuscript

action.text: Inspect every healing field wound at least once daily for spreading redness, increasing warmth, worsening throbbing pain, swelling, foul odor, or yellow/green pus drainage.
Outline the outer edge of any skin redness lightly with a pen and note the time so you can see objectively whether redness is expanding outward over subsequent hours.
Treat red streaks traveling up a limb, fever, chills, shaking, rapid breathing, or new confusion as urgent systemic infection emergencies requiring immediate evacuation and clinical antibiotics.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Catch localized skin infection early and trigger urgent evacuation before systemic bloodstream infection develops.
applies: Any cut, blister, burn, splinter, or bite monitored over hours to days in remote settings.
equipment: Clean pen to trace redness borders, watch/log, clean dry dressings, and emergency comms.

failure.text: Waiting three days on a multi-day trip while redness climbs past the ankle and fever begins, assuming basic ointment will cure a deep infection.

verify.text: Confirm wound appearance, pen-border progress, and presence or absence of fever/chills are logged daily.

stop.text: Expanding redness past marked lines, pus, joint stiffness, red streaks, fever, or confusion mandate immediate exit to medical care.

diagram: Mark redness border & log time | Watch pus, heat, pain & red streaks | Fever or streaks -> urgent clinical exit
visual: Time-progression infection timeline distinguishing normal clean healing from localized worsening, red streaking, and urgent systemic emergency. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Cool minor thermal burns with cool water and protect intact blisters
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Burns; new manuscript

action.text: Stop the burning process immediately, remove watches, rings, belts, and loose non-stuck clothing near the burn before swelling starts, and cool the minor burn under cool running potable water for 10 to 20 minutes.
Never apply ice, snow, butter, cooking oil, toothpaste, or unapproved ointments to a fresh burn—ice deepens tissue damage and greasy substances trap heat and bacteria.
Cover the cooled burn loosely with clean non-stick sterile gauze, keep intact burn blisters unbroken as a natural sterile barrier, and keep the patient warm overall to prevent hypothermia.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Halt thermal tissue injury safely on small superficial burns while preventing secondary infection and cold injury.
applies: Small, superficial flame, hot-pot, or steam scald burns without deep charring or high-risk body zones.
equipment: Cool (not icy) clean potable water, clean non-stick sterile gauze, and dry insulating layers for the rest of the body.

failure.text: Packing snow directly onto a camp-stove scald or popping intact blisters with a pocketknife in dirty camp conditions.

verify.text: Confirm rings/tight gear are removed, cooling used cool (not icy) water, blisters remain intact, and dressing is loose and clean.

stop.text: Any worsening blistering, deep pale/charred skin, high-risk zone involvement, or uncontrolled pain escalates immediately to clinical burn care.

diagram: Remove rings & cool with cool water | Never apply ice, grease or pop blisters | Cover loosely clean; monitor warmth
visual: Correct versus incorrect minor burn care contrasting cool potable water and loose non-stick dressings against ice, grease, and blister popping. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Escalate major, deep, airway, or high-risk-zone burns to emergency care
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Burns; new manuscript

action.text: Call 911 immediately for ANY burn that is large (larger than the patient's palm on high-risk zones or extensive body area), deep (waxy white, brown, charred, or painless), or involves the face, eyes, hands, feet, groin, major joints, or completely encircles a limb/chest.
Treat singed nose hairs, soot around the mouth/nose, hoarse voice, coughing, or breathing difficulty after fire/smoke exposure as a potential airway-swelling emergency requiring immediate EMS.

Do NOT pull clothing stuck to burned skin and do NOT immerse massive body burns in cold water (which triggers rapid hypothermia); cover loosely with clean dry dressings, insulate against shock, and keep NPO.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Identify burn patterns that threaten airways, circulation, function, or life and initiate immediate 911 evacuation.
applies: Large burns, deep white/leathery/charred burns, smoke/flame inhalation, or burns involving critical anatomical zones.
equipment: Clean dry sterile sheets/dressings, ground insulation, blankets, and emergency communication.

failure.text: Dousing a large torso burn repeatedly in cold lake water until the patient develops severe hypothermia, or ignoring hoarse voice after a stove flare-up.

verify.text: Confirm airway sounds/voice are monitored continuously, stuck clothing is left undisturbed, body heat is preserved, and 911/EMS is dispatched.

stop.text: Any hoarseness, breathing labor, circumferential tightness, or shock signs require maximum-priority medical evacuation.

diagram: Face/hand/foot/joint/deep/large burn | Watch airway soot & hoarseness | Dry loose cover, warmth & urgent 911
visual: Conceptual anatomical orientation guide highlighting automatic clinical-escalation burn zones (airway, face, hands, feet, joints, circumferential). Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Handle chemical and electrical burns with scene isolation before care
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Burns and Poison Control; new manuscript

action.text: For electrical injury, NEVER touch the person until the power source is confirmed shut off by utility/breaker controls (stay well back from downed power lines and call 911); remember electrical burns cause severe hidden internal tissue and heart-rhythm damage even with tiny skin marks.

For dry chemical powders on skin, brush loose dry powder off with gloved hands or cloth BEFORE flushing continuously with copious cool running water for at least 20 minutes while removing contaminated clothing.
Call 911 for ALL electrical burns, chemical eye splashes, large/painful chemical burns, or breathing irritation, and save the exact chemical label for Poison Control/EMS.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Protect rescuers from live electrical current or hazardous chemicals while initiating safe flushing and clinical escalation.
applies: Fuel/battery/caustic chemical skin splashes or contact with energized wiring, generators, or lightning.
equipment: Dry non-conductive isolation awareness, clean running water, protective gloves, and Poison Control / 911 contact.

failure.text: Grabbing a person still touching an energized generator cord, or pouring a tiny cup of water onto dry caustic lime powder so it activates and spreads across skin.

verify.text: Confirm power or chemical source is isolated, rescuers avoided contamination, and exact chemical identity or voltage context is logged for EMS.

stop.text: Any electrical contact, loss of consciousness, chest pain, or chemical eye/airway exposure requires immediate emergency medical evaluation.

diagram: Isolate power or brush dry chemical | Flush liquid chemical 20+ min clean | All electrical & eye exposures -> 911
visual: System boundary diagram separating live electrical/chemical hazard zone from safe gloved brush-and-flush decontamination and 911 transfer. Conceptual, not to scale.
reviewer: Burn care, occupational safety, and toxicology

title: Practice field caregiver hygiene and body-fluid barrier precautions
origin: CDC Safe Water and USDA/CDC Hand Hygiene; new manuscript

action.text: Put on clean disposable nitrile gloves (or clean plastic-bag barriers if gloves are absent) before touching blood, open wounds, vomit, or body fluids, and wash hands thoroughly before and after patient care.

Remove soiled gloves carefully from the inside out without snapping droplets onto skin or eyes, seal blood- or waste-soaked items in double leak-proof bags for proper pack-out/disposal, and wash hands immediately afterward.
Keep wound-care water, patient utensils, and latrine/waste zones strictly separate from group drinking water and food preparation areas.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent cross-contamination between wounds, fecal-oral germs, and bloodborne exposures during remote patient care.
applies: Every first-aid interaction, multi-day group camp care, and remote illness management.
equipment: Disposable nitrile gloves, soap and confirmed potable water, alcohol-based hand rub (≥60% alcohol), and sealed waste bag.

failure.text: Handling bloody dressings bare-handed and immediately preparing group food without washing hands with soap and safe water.

verify.text: Confirm caregivers washed hands with soap/potable water (or hand rub when not visibly soiled) and sealed bio-waste separately from food/gear.

stop.text: If blood or body fluids splash into a caregiver's eyes, mouth, or broken skin, flush immediately with clean potable water and seek prompt clinical post-exposure evaluation.

diagram: Barrier gloves before body fluids | Peel inside-out & double-bag waste | Wash hands with soap & safe water
visual: Four-step caregiver hygiene plate covering barrier donning, clean-to-dirty separation, inside-out glove removal, and potable handwashing. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Prevent and protect friction blisters and foot-skin breakdown
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Wounds; new manuscript

action.text: Stop immediately at the very first warm stinging "hot spot" on a heel or toe—air and dry the foot, change into dry socks, remove grit from boots, and place smooth friction-reducing tape or donut padding around the spot.

Keep intact fluid-filled blisters unbroken whenever possible because intact roof skin is the body's best sterile dressing; if a blister tears open on its own, rinse gently with clean potable water, leave loose skin flat if clean, and cover with sterile non-stick dressing.
Treat ANY foot wound, blister, or skin crack in a person with diabetes, neuropathy, or poor circulation as a high-risk medical issue requiring strict protection and early clinical inspection.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Catch footwear friction hot spots before skin tears and recognize high-risk foot infections that halt backcountry travel.
applies: Multi-day hiking, wet-trail portaging, snowshoeing, or heavy-pack travel.
equipment: Dry spare wool/synthetic socks, breathable blister tape/moleskin, clean gauze, and potable water.

failure.text: Ignoring a burning heel hot spot for five miles until raw torn skin fills with trail mud and becomes infected.

verify.text: Confirm feet are inspected dry at every camp stop and no spreading redness, pus, or worsening limp is developing.

stop.text: Spreading redness, warmth, pus, inability to walk normally, or any foot breakdown in a diabetic traveler requires halting the trip and seeking clinical evaluation.

diagram: Stop at first hot spot; dry & pad | Keep intact blisters unbroken & clean | Watch infection & diabetic foot flags
visual: Failure-mode diagram tracing ignored footwear friction through torn contaminated blister to early hot-spot padding and infection exit thresholds. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Identify concussion symptoms and enforce strict stop-activity observation
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Head Injuries; new manuscript

action.text: Stop physical travel, climbing, paddling, or hazardous tasks immediately after any head impact causing brief dazing, headache, dizziness, nausea, balance wobble, confusion, memory gaps, or sensitivity to light/noise—even without loss of consciousness.
Keep a responsible companion observing the person continuously for worsening symptoms over the next several hours, logging mental clarity, speech, and headache trends on paper.
Never allow a person with suspected concussion to return to risky terrain, drive a vehicle, or travel alone; arrange supervised exit and medical clearance.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize mild traumatic brain injury after falls or head strikes and prevent dangerous second impacts.
applies: Any bump, blow, fall, or jarring impact to the head or body followed by subtle mental or physical changes.
equipment: Written symptom-monitoring sheet, shade/shelter, and buddy watch.

failure.text: Letting a hiker who "only saw stars for a second" after slipping on wet rock continue scrambling an exposed ridge alone.

verify.text: Confirm hazardous activity stopped immediately, a buddy is watching continuously, and baseline orientation questions are recorded with times.

stop.text: Any worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, or balance decline transitions immediately to urgent 911 head-trauma evacuation.

diagram: Any head impact + dazed/headache | Stop risky travel; continuous buddy watch | Escalate 911 if any symptom worsens
visual: Time-progression concussion observation timeline separating immediate stop-activity, hourly red-flag rechecks, supervised exit, and 911 escalation triggers. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Escalate severe head-trauma red flags as urgent neurosurgical emergencies
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Head Injuries; new manuscript

action.text: Activate 911/SAR immediately for ANY severe head-injury red flag: loss of consciousness (even brief), repeated vomiting, worsening severe headache, confusion/agitation, slurred speech, weakness/numbness, seizure, unequal pupils, or clear fluid/blood draining from ears or nose.

Keep the person lying still with head and neck gently supported in line, control external scalp bleeding with gentle pressure (never pressing hard into a depressed or soft skull area), and keep them warm and strictly NPO.
Monitor airway and breathing continuously; if vomiting occurs, carefully log-roll the entire body as one aligned unit onto the side to clear the mouth while protecting the neck.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Detect rising intracranial danger early so evacuation is launched before fatal neurological decline occurs.
applies: High-force falls, falling tree limbs, vehicle/watercraft strikes, or any head injury showing red-flag progression.
equipment: Spinal-stabilization awareness, ground insulation, written trend log, and emergency communications.

failure.text: Letting a head-injured companion "sleep it off" in a tent after vomiting twice and becoming hard to wake.

verify.text: Confirm exact time of impact, responsiveness level, and any red-flag progression are transmitted clearly to EMS/SAR.

stop.text: Any loss of consciousness, declining alertness, vomiting, or uneven pupils requires immediate highest-priority emergency extraction.

diagram: LOC, vomiting, confusion, ear/nose fluid | Hold head/neck still; gentle scalp press | Urgent 911/SAR; never "sleep it off"
visual: Three-tier head-injury escalation ladder distinguishing observed mild concussion from red-flag EMS activation and airway-protected log-roll. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Maintain spinal motion restriction after high-force falls or impacts
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Head Injuries and Fractures; new manuscript

action.text: Instruct an alert patient immediately to stay completely still and look straight ahead—do NOT twist, nod, sit up, or let bystanders pull them to their feet after a high-mechanism impact.
Gently stabilize the head in the neutral position found using hands or snug rolled clothing beside the ears (never force a crooked neck straight or apply traction) while activating 911/SAR.
Check whether the patient can feel and wiggle fingers and toes without moving their spine, keep them protected from wind/cold, and leave definitive spinal packaging to trained EMS crews.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Minimize secondary spinal-cord injury by keeping an injured person's head, neck, and back still until EMS arrives.
applies: Falls from height, diving into shallow water, falling tree limbs, sled/snowmobile/bike crashes, or any neck/back pain or tingling after trauma.
equipment: Rolled jackets/packs for gentle side-of-head cushioning, ground insulation where reachable without shifting, and emergency comms.

failure.text: Pulling a fallen climber upright to "check if they can walk" when they complain of midline neck pain and numb fingers.

verify.text: Confirm the head and spine remained unmoved, sensation/movement in extremities was noted, and EMS knows spinal precautions are active.

stop.text: Move a suspected spinal-injury patient ONLY if immediate life-threatening scene danger or airway obstruction makes staying put fatal.

diagram: High fall / neck pain / tingling | Hold head & neck still as found | Wait for trained EMS packaging
visual: Correct versus incorrect spinal care contrasting neutral in-place stabilization and EMS activation against pulling the patient upright or twisting the neck. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Immobilize suspected limb fractures in the position found
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Fractures; new manuscript

action.text: Expose the injured area gently to check for open wounds or deformity, remove rings/watches early before swelling tightens, and support the limb steadily in the exact position found—do NOT attempt to snap or force visibly deformed bones straight.

Pad all bony prominences and natural hollows generously, secure a splint wide enough to immobilize the joint ABOVE and the joint BELOW the suspected fracture (or bones above/below an injured joint), and tie snug—never tight enough to choke circulation.
Check warmth, color, sensation, and gentle toe/finger movement beyond the splint immediately after tying, and arrange clinical X-ray evaluation.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Reduce pain, tissue damage, and internal bleeding by splinting suspected broken arms or legs safely without lay straightening.
applies: Suspected forearm, wrist, lower-leg, or collarbone fractures with swelling, localized bone tenderness, or inability to use the limb.
equipment: Soft padding (jackets, foam pad), rigid or semi-rigid supports (commercial SAM splint, folded pad), and wide cloth ties/bandages.

failure.text: Tying narrow paracord directly over the fracture site without padding or attempting to yank an angulated forearm straight in camp.

verify.text: Confirm padding cushions all gaps, ties sit above/below the break (not over it), and circulation/sensation beyond the splint remain intact.

stop.text: Cold pale/blue fingers or toes, numbness, open bone, or severe uncontrollable pain requires loosening tight ties immediately and activating urgent EMS.

diagram: Support limb as found; remove rings | Pad well & immobilize above/below | Verify circulation & evacuate for X-ray
visual: Conceptual limb-splint schematic illustrating padded support spanning joints above and below the fracture with distal CSM check points. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Monitor distal circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) after splinting
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Fractures; new manuscript

action.text: Before applying any splint or wrap—and again immediately after securing it—compare the injured hand or foot against the uninjured side for skin warmth/pink color (Circulation), light-touch feeling (Sensation), and gentle finger/toe wiggle (Movement).
Leave fingertips or toes visibly exposed at the end of every splint or wrap so you can recheck CSM every 15 to 30 minutes as swelling progresses.
If fingers or toes turn cold, pale, bluish, numb, tingling, or intensely throbbing under a wrap, loosen the ties immediately and recheck within minutes.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Detect dangerous swelling or tight bandages early before restricted blood flow causes permanent limb damage.
applies: Every splinted, wrapped, or swollen extremity injury monitored during backcountry waiting or exit.
equipment: Watch and written patient log.

failure.text: Wrapping a swollen ankle tightly inside an opaque boot and never checking cold numb toes over a three-hour hike out.

verify.text: Confirm baseline and repeated timed CSM checks (warm/pink, normal touch, intact wiggle) are recorded on the patient log.

stop.text: Persistent loss of warmth, color, or sensation even after loosening wraps is a limb-threatening emergency requiring urgent EMS transport.

diagram: Check CSM before & after splinting | Keep fingers/toes exposed to view | Cold/numb/pale -> loosen & urgent EMS
visual: Four-step neurovascular check plate mapping baseline CSM, exposed-digit splinting, 15–30 min rechecks, and urgent loosen/escalate trigger. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Protect open fractures from contamination and expedite urgent EMS
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Fractures and Wounds; new manuscript

action.text: Activate 911/SAR immediately—open fractures carry high risk of severe bleeding, deep bone infection, and permanent limb loss requiring urgent hospital surgery and IV antibiotics.
Control active external bleeding with gentle clean gauze pressure around the wound edges without pressing directly on exposed bone fragments, and NEVER push protruding bone back beneath the skin.
Cover exposed bone and tissue gently with clean sterile dressing, pad and immobilize the limb in the position found, insulate the patient against shock, and keep strictly NPO.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Manage life- and limb-threatening open (compound) fractures safely without pushing bone ends back inside the wound.
applies: Any suspected fracture where bone breaks through the skin or an open wound communicates directly with a fracture site.
equipment: Clean sterile moist/dry gauze dressings, gloves, padding, and emergency communications.

failure.text: Attempting to rinse deeply or push an exposed tibia back under the skin in camp, driving dirt deep into the bone marrow.

verify.text: Confirm bleeding is controlled gently around edges, sterile cover protects exposed tissue, distal CSM is checked, and EMS is inbound.

stop.text: Heavy bleeding uncontrolled by gentle pressure, cold pale extremity, or shock signs trigger immediate maximum-priority trauma escalation.

diagram: Exposed bone -> call 911 immediately | Never push bone back; cover sterile | Immobilize as found & treat for shock
visual: Correct versus incorrect open-fracture care contrasting sterile cover and gentle edge pressure against pushing bone inward or rough alignment. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Treat suspected pelvis or femur fractures as life-threatening shock emergencies
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Fractures and Shock; new manuscript

action.text: Activate 911/SAR immediately for suspected pelvic or femur fracture—both can bleed rapidly into deep internal compartments and trigger fatal hemorrhagic shock without visible external blood.

Keep the person completely flat and still where found, do NOT rock or squeeze the pelvis repeatedly to "test stability," and place soft padding gently beside the legs and hips for comfort without rolling the patient.
Insulate heavily against cold ground, keep strictly NPO, monitor mental status and breathing continuously, and await trained EMS/SAR extraction teams.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize massive internal bleeding risk in hip, pelvis, or thigh-bone trauma and enforce strict immobility and EMS activation.
applies: High-force falls, crush injuries, or impacts causing severe hip, groin, pelvic, or mid-thigh pain and inability to move or bear weight.
equipment: Ground insulation, blankets, soft side padding, and emergency communications.

failure.text: Trying to help a hiker with severe hip/pelvis pain stand up and hop to a vehicle, disrupting a fragile internal pelvic clot.

verify.text: Confirm the patient remained flat and still, zero pelvic-rocking tests were performed, warmth is maintained, and SAR knows urgent trauma carry is needed.

stop.text: Any worsening pallor, restlessness, confusion, or rapid breathing signals active internal shock demanding immediate dispatch update.

diagram: High-force hip/pelvis/thigh pain | Zero standing or pelvic-rock tests | Keep flat, warm, NPO & urgent 911
visual: Escalation ladder distinguishing stable minor extremity injuries from non-ambulatory pelvis/femur internal-hemorrhage emergencies. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Evaluate sprains and strains conservatively without ruling out hidden fractures
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Sprains and Strains; new manuscript

action.text: Halt travel promptly, inspect the joint for deformity, severe bone-edge tenderness, or numbness, and protect the joint with rest, gentle comfortable compression wrap (never tight), and elevation when resting.

Remember that severe sprains and hairline/undisplaced fractures feel identical in the field—only a clinical X-ray can rule out a fracture; never force a traveler to walk on a joint that buckles or cannot bear weight.
Check distal warmth, color, and toe/finger sensation repeatedly after wrapping, and plan an assisted exit or SAR call if the terrain or pain prevents safe weight-bearing.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Support joint sprains safely while recognizing when inability to bear weight requires clinical X-ray rather than field assumptions.
applies: Twisted ankles, knees, or wrists without visible deformity, open wounds, or loss of circulation.
equipment: Elastic wrap or supportive tape, cool compress/water, padded brace/pole if walking out, and dry socks.

failure.text: Assuming a massively swollen ankle is "just a sprain" and marching five downhill miles on an undisplaced fibula fracture.

verify.text: Confirm CSM remains intact below any wrap, bony-edge tenderness was noted, and exit mode matches actual safe mobility.

stop.text: Visible deformity, bone-point pain, numbness, cold toes, or inability to take four controlled weight-bearing steps requires immobilization and non-weight-bearing evacuation.

diagram: Rest, protect & comfortable support | Field exam cannot rule out fracture | Cannot bear weight -> immobilize & exit
visual: Decision tree evaluating deformity, bone tenderness, CSM, and safe weight-bearing to distinguish controlled exit from non-weight-bearing rescue. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Support suspected joint dislocations in comfort without lay reduction attempts
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Fractures and Sprains; new manuscript

action.text: Immobilize a suspected dislocated shoulder, elbow, kneecap, hip, or finger gently in the position of greatest comfort using padded slings or pillows—do NOT yank or attempt lay joint reduction in the field.
Check distal circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) immediately and repeatedly; knee and hip dislocations carry especially high artery-injury risk requiring urgent EMS transport.
Keep the patient warm, withhold food/water if surgical sedation may be needed at the hospital, and arrange prompt clinical orthopedic evaluation.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Protect nerves and blood vessels around a dislocated shoulder, knee, or finger by immobilizing in the position of comfort for clinical care.
applies: Visible joint step-off, locked joint range, or sudden severe joint pain after a fall or wrenching force.
equipment: Soft sling/swathe or padded splint cushions, watch, and emergency communications.

failure.text: Having untrained bystanders tug forcefully on a dislocated arm or knee, trapping an artery or fracturing the joint rim.

verify.text: Confirm the joint is cushioned comfortably as found, distal CSM is logged, and clinical evacuation is underway.

stop.text: Any pale, cold, pulseless, or numb extremity beyond a dislocated joint is a limb-threatening emergency requiring immediate 911 activation.

diagram: Locked/deformed joint -> pad as found | Never yank or reduce in lay care | Check distal CSM & urgent clinical care
visual: Correct versus incorrect dislocation care contrasting cushioned sling/pad stabilization and CSM monitoring against risky untrained pulling. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Flush chemical splashes and loose surface grit gently from eyes
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Eye Injuries; new manuscript

action.text: For chemical splashes, start flushing immediately with copious gentle streams of clean potable water or sterile saline for at least 15 to 20 continuous minutes, tilting the head so rinse water drains OUTWARD away from the unaffected eye.
Remove contact lenses gently if they do not flush out on their own (never force a stuck lens), instruct the person NOT to rub the eye, and keep eyelids gently held open during chemical irrigation.
Seek urgent medical/ophthalmology evaluation for ALL chemical eye splashes, persistent grit feeling after gentle flushing, blurred vision, or severe light sensitivity.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Dilute corrosive splashes or flush loose dust safely without scratching the cornea or delaying urgent eye care.
applies: Soap, stove fuel, sanitizer, insect-repellent splashes, or loose windblown dust/ash in the eye (no embedded sharp object).
equipment: Clean potable water or sterile saline eyewash, clean cup/squeeze bottle, and emergency contacts.

failure.text: Rubbing a gritty eye vigorously (scratching the cornea) or flushing a chemical splash across the nose bridge into the healthy eye.

verify.text: Confirm outward drainage away from the clean eye, full 15–20 minute flush for chemicals, and zero rubbing.

stop.text: Any chemical splash, vision loss, severe pain, or object stuck on the eyeball surface halts travel and requires immediate clinical eye care.

diagram: Tilt injured eye downward/outward | Flush clean water 15–20 min gentle | Zero rubbing; urgent eye evaluation
visual: Four-step eye irrigation plate showing outward tilt away from the clean eye, continuous potable flushing, zero rubbing, and clinical referral. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Shield blunt or penetrating eye trauma without applying pressure
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Eye Injuries; new manuscript

action.text: Never press on an injured eyeball, never flush a suspected ruptured/penetrated globe, and NEVER pull out any embedded splinter, thorn, glass, or fishhook from the eye.

Tape a rigid dome shield (such as the clean bottom of a paper cup or commercial shield) gently over the bony brow and cheekbone so NOTHING touches the eyelids or protruding object, and ask the patient to keep both eyes calm and still to reduce synchronized eye movement.
Keep the patient sitting slightly upright if comfortable, keep NPO for potential surgery, and evacuate immediately to emergency ophthalmology care.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent catastrophic vision loss from eyeball pressure or removal of embedded objects after sharp or blunt eye strikes.
applies: Branch pokes, flying metal/wood chips, fishing hooks, or hard blunt blows to the eye socket with pain, blood, or vision change.
equipment: Rigid makeshift eye shield (clean paper cup bottom or commercial eye shield), tape, and emergency communications.

failure.text: Packing tight gauze pressure directly over a branch-punctured eye or trying to pull a barbed fishhook out in the field.

verify.text: Confirm rigid shield rests only on surrounding bone with zero eyelid contact, embedded objects remain untouched, and urgent EMS/transport is active.

stop.text: Any penetrating object, visible blood inside the colored iris, double vision, or vision loss is an immediate sight-saving emergency.

diagram: Never press or pull embedded objects | Tape rigid dome onto surrounding bone | Keep eyes calm; urgent ophthalmology
visual: Cutaway eye-shield boundary showing rigid cup resting strictly on brow and cheekbone with zero contact on the injured globe. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Spot chest and acute abdominal emergencies requiring immediate evacuation
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Wounds and Shock; new manuscript

action.text: Call 911 immediately for chest injury causing shortness of breath, coughing blood, uneven chest movement, or an open sucking chest wound (leave an open chest wound uncovered/vented unless trained specifically in vented chest-seal care; never seal tightly with improvised airtight plastic that traps air pressure).

Treat severe localized or worsening abdominal pain, a hard board-like abdomen, persistent vomiting, high fever, blood in vomit/stool, or pregnancy abdominal pain/bleeding as urgent surgical/medical emergencies requiring evacuation.

Position the patient comfortably (often slightly upright for chest pain or knees gently bent for abdominal pain), insulate from cold ground, and withhold food, water, and painkillers that mask deterioration.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize life-threatening chest wall, breathing, and abdominal warning signs that cannot be managed in backcountry settings.
applies: Fall onto ribs, chest puncture, sudden severe abdominal pain, rigid belly, or persistent vomiting with fever.
equipment: Clean dressings, ground insulation, monitoring log, and emergency communication.

failure.text: Sealing an open chest wound tightly on all four sides with duct tape without venting, or giving heavy pain pills for worsening lower-right abdominal pain and waiting overnight.

verify.text: Confirm breathing effort, abdominal rigidity/pain trend, and NPO status are logged clearly for incoming EMS.

stop.text: Rapidly worsening shortness of breath, bluish lips, rigid abdomen, or shock signs require maximum-priority emergency extraction.

diagram: Rib/chest labor or rigid painful belly | Comfort posture, warmth & strictly NPO | Urgent 911; zero airtight tape seals
visual: Three-tier torso-emergency escalation ladder distinguishing minor bruised ribs from breathing distress, open chest wounds, and acute surgical abdomen. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Recognize mild hypothermia and halt heat loss before judgment fails
origin: B012-P07 hypothermia signs and CDC Preventing Hypothermia; adapted historical material

action.text: Watch for early mild hypothermia cues—vigorous shivering, cold hands losing fine dexterity ("umbles": grumbles, fumbles, mumbles, stumbles), and withdrawn mood—and stop travel IMMEDIATELY before confusion deepens.
Move out of wind and wet exposure into shelter, insulate underneath with a thick pad, replace wet garments with dry wool/synthetic layers and hat, and wrap in a dry sleeping bag.

If the person is completely alert, oriented, and swallowing normally, offer warm (not scalding) sweet drinks and quick calories—never alcohol or tobacco—and keep monitoring until shivering stops and warmth stabilizes.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Catch early shivering and mild clumsiness while the patient can still cooperate with dry shelter and active rewarming.
applies: Cool, wet, windy, or winter conditions—remembering hypothermia occurs well above freezing when wet and chilled.
equipment: Dry insulating layers, windproof shell, sleeping pad, sleeping bag, wind shelter, and warm sweet liquids (ONLY if fully alert).

failure.text: Pushing a shivering, fumbling hiker another two miles toward the car in cold rain instead of stopping immediately to shelter and dry them.

verify.text: Confirm wind/wet exposure is stopped, dry layers and ground pad are in place, and mental clarity is improving across timed checks.

stop.text: Slurred speech, confusion, drowsiness, or shivering that stops while the person remains cold indicates moderate-to-severe hypothermia requiring immediate 911 evacuation.

diagram: Spot shivering & early "umbles" | Stop travel; dry layers & ground pad | Warm sweet sips only if fully alert
visual: Four-step mild hypothermia intervention plate mapping early recognition, shelter/dry swap, ground insulation, and alert oral rewarming. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Handle moderate-to-severe hypothermia gently and protect core warmth
origin: B012-P08 severe hypothermia and CDC Preventing Hypothermia; adapted historical material

action.text: Activate 911/SAR immediately and treat the patient as critically fragile—keep them HORIZONTAL and handle them extremely gently (no vigorous rubbing, rough standing, or sudden jostling, which can trigger lethal heart arrhythmias in a cold heart).

Protect from all further heat loss by cutting away wet clothing gently if inside shelter, placing thick insulation underneath and all around the body (hypothermia wrap), and covering the head and neck.

Apply gentle insulated external warmth ONLY to the trunk (armpits, chest, groin—never direct scalding heat or hot immersion of arms/legs), withhold oral fluids if confused or drowsy, and monitor breathing carefully for a full minute before deciding on CPR per dispatcher guidance.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Stabilize a confused, drowsy, or non-shivering hypothermic patient without triggering fatal cardiac arrest during movement.
applies: Cold-exposed patient exhibiting confusion, slurred speech, stumbling, drowsiness, unresponsiveness, or stopped shivering while still cold.
equipment: Thick ground insulation, dry vapor-barrier/sleeping-bag wrap, gentle warm packs wrapped in cloth (trunk only), and emergency comms.

failure.text: Forcing a confused, non-shivering hypothermic victim to stand up and walk, or dunking their limbs in hot water.

verify.text: Confirm patient stays horizontal, wrapped against ground/wind loss, zero oral fluids given while altered, and urgent EMS transport is active.

stop.text: Unresponsiveness with absent normal breathing triggers immediate dispatcher-guided CPR and continuous evacuation until hospital rewarming.

diagram: Confusion/no shiver -> severe emergency | Keep horizontal & handle ultra-gently | Wrap dry, warm trunk only & call 911
visual: Conceptual core-thermal zone diagram showing horizontal full-body insulation wrap, gentle trunk-only heat packs, and strict extremity/jostling exclusions. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Stabilize cold-water immersion survivors and guard against post-rescue collapse
origin: B013-P08 post-immersion care and MN DNR Cold Water Safety; adapted historical material

action.text: Call 911 immediately after any cold-water immersion, move the survivor gently out of wind into shelter, and keep them lying horizontal rather than letting them walk vigorously right after exit.

Remove soaked clothing gently (cutting it off if movement causes strain), pat skin dry without vigorous rubbing, insulate heavily underneath and around the torso and head, and monitor breathing and mental clarity continuously.
Watch closely for delayed deterioration ("circum-rescue collapse" or continued core cooling) and potential water aspiration even if the person initially insists they feel fine.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Protect a person pulled from icy or cold water from silent post-exit cooling, shock, and sudden collapse.
applies: Anyone pulled from cold lakes, rivers, ice breakthroughs, or swamped watercraft—even if initially talking.
equipment: Windproof shelter or heated building/vehicle, thick ground pad, dry blankets/layers, and 911 dispatch contact.

failure.text: Letting someone who fell through lake ice walk a mile back to a cabin in wet clothes because they initially feel adrenaline-warm.

verify.text: Confirm survivor is horizontal, dry-wrapped out of wind, monitored continuously, and medically evaluated by EMS.

stop.text: Any shivering cessation, confusion, coughing/breathing labor, or faintness escalates immediately to emergency resuscitation readiness and urgent transport.

diagram: Pull to shelter & keep horizontal | Cut off wet clothes; wrap core dry | Call 911; watch delayed collapse
visual: System boundary diagram tracing post-immersion wet-wind cooling versus dry horizontal hypothermia wrap and continuous EMS monitoring. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Monitor submersion survivors for delayed breathing deterioration
origin: B013-P18 submersion care and American Red Cross; adapted historical material

action.text: Activate 911 immediately for ANY submersion involving loss of consciousness, cessation of breathing, persistent coughing, foamy sputum, chest discomfort, or blue lips; if unresponsive and not breathing normally, start trained/dispatcher CPR immediately.

Even when a submerged person exits coughing and alert, remove wet layers, keep them resting warmly, and arrange prompt clinical medical evaluation—aspirated water can irritate lung linings and cause worsening breathing distress over subsequent hours.
Do NOT attempt abdominal thrusts or turn a person upside down to "drain water from lungs"—that delays ventilation and triggers vomiting and aspiration.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Recognize that water aspiration during near-drowning requires medical evaluation even after the person resumes coughing and talking.
applies: Anyone submerged, dunked under ice or surf, or who inhaled water during a cold-water incident.
equipment: Dry insulating shelter, watch, written monitoring log, and 911 communications.

failure.text: Sending a child or paddler home to nap after a brief near-drowning episode without medical assessment while persistent coughing worsens.

verify.text: Confirm breathing rate, cough severity, mental clarity, and medical evaluation plan are documented and communicated.

stop.text: Any worsening cough, fast labored breathing, chest pain, extreme fatigue, or confusion after submersion requires immediate 911 transport.

diagram: Any submersion -> assess breath & 911 | Never press belly to "drain water" | Monitor hours; clinical lung evaluation
visual: Correct versus incorrect submersion care contrasting warm rest, dispatcher CPR if non-breathing, and clinical lung review against harmful lung-draining maneuvers. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Distinguish early frostnip from superficial and deep frostbite
origin: B012-P24 frostbite signs and WMS 2024 Frostbite Guideline; adapted historical material

action.text: Watch buddies' cheeks, nose, and ears frequently—early frostnip shows pale/red cold skin with stinging or tingling that remains soft and pliable and responds promptly to shelter and gentle skin-to-skin warmth (such as tucking bare fingers into your own armpit).

Recognize true frostbite cues: waxy white, grayish, or mottled skin, numbness ("wooden" loss of feeling), and firm or hard-frozen underlying tissue—remembering field inspection cannot reliably determine final tissue depth.
Stop exposed travel immediately upon finding numb or waxy skin, shield from wind, remove rings/watches/tight boots before swelling begins, and never rub frozen skin with snow or bare hands.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Catch reversible cold-skin warning cues early and recognize true freezing injury before tissue loss deepens.
applies: Sub-freezing air, wind chill, metal/fuel contact, or wet winter gloves/boots affecting fingers, toes, ears, nose, or cheeks.
equipment: Windproof shelter, dry mittens/socks, buddy face-check routine, and warm trunk-contact awareness.

failure.text: Ignoring numb toes inside damp boots for hours or rubbing white waxy cheeks with snow, which mechanically shreds frozen skin cells.

verify.text: Confirm buddy face/hand checks occurred, jewelry/tight items are removed, and wind exposure has stopped.

stop.text: Numb waxy or hard-frozen skin requires immediate trip abort, protection from trauma/refreezing, and clinical frostbite evaluation.

diagram: Frostnip: soft, tingly -> warm gently | Frostbite: waxy, numb, firm -> abort | Never rub with snow or dry flame
visual: Three-tier cold-injury escalation ladder contrasting reversible frostnip from superficial/deep frostbite protection and hospital care. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Protect frostbitten tissue and obey the strict non-refreezing rule
origin: B012-P25 frostbite field limits and WMS 2024 Frostbite Guideline; adapted historical material

action.text: Keep frozen tissue protected from crushing, friction, and impact—do NOT actively thaw frostbitten feet or hands in the field if ANY chance of refreezing exists before reaching definitive clinical care, because a thaw-refreeze cycle causes devastating tissue necrosis.
Never hold numb frostbitten tissue near campfires, stoves, car heaters, or exhaust pipes—loss of sensation allows severe deep thermal burns without pain warning.

If safe definitive shelter and rapid transport with ZERO refreezing risk exist, follow qualified clinical/WMS controlled warm-water rewarming protocols (clean circulating water ~98–102°F), cushion gently between digits with dry sterile gauze without popping blisters, and transport promptly.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Prevent catastrophic tissue loss by avoiding thaw-refreeze cycles and dry-heat burns during backcountry evacuation.
applies: Suspected frozen digits, feet, or facial tissue outside immediate hospital care.
equipment: Dry bulky sterile gauze, clean padding between digits, loose warm dry insulation, and evacuation plan.

failure.text: Thawing frozen toes over a camp stove, then putting cold wet boots back on to hike out so the thawed tissue refreezes solid.

verify.text: Confirm zero refreezing risk before any thaw, zero dry-flame heat exposure, and clean padded digit separation for evacuation.

stop.text: Frozen extremities require immediate evacuation to clinical care; walking on thawed, swollen, blistered feet risks massive tissue destruction.

diagram: Refreeze risk -> protect frozen & exit | Never use stoves/flames on numb skin | Zero refreeze -> controlled warm thaw + MD
visual: Decision tree evaluating refreeze risk during evacuation to separate protected-frozen transport from controlled warm-water rewarming and hospital care. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Prevent and recognize non-freezing cold injury (trench foot)
origin: CDC Preventing Hypothermia and NPS Wetlands Safety; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize that immersion/trench foot develops from prolonged wet cold WITHOUT freezing—feet turn cold, pale, wrinkled, numb, or tingling, then swell, throb, redden, and blister painfully upon warming.
Prevent injury by changing into dry socks at least daily, airing and drying feet completely at camp, warming boots/insoles away from direct flame, and never sleeping in damp footwear.

If trench foot signs appear, remove wet boots/socks immediately, dry feet gently without rubbing or soaking in hot water, keep feet clean, warm, dry, and elevated in shelter, and arrange non-weight-bearing evacuation for clinical care.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Catch prolonged wet-cold foot injury occurring well above freezing before nerve and skin damage disables walking.
applies: Multi-day travel or standing in cold rain, slush, wetlands, or damp boots at temperatures between roughly 32°F and 60°F.
equipment: Multiple pairs of dry wool/synthetic socks, breathable camp footwear, dry towel, and sheltered warm sleeping setup.

failure.text: Wearing waterlogged boots for three straight cold autumn days without airing or changing socks until feet swell too large to fit back inside footwear.

verify.text: Confirm daily dry-foot inspection, spare dry socks packed waterproof, and absence of numbness, mottling, or painful swelling.

stop.text: Persistent numbness, swelling, purple/pale mottling, or painful blistering halts hiking and requires medical evaluation.

diagram: Wet cold above 32°F harms nerves | Air, dry & swap socks every camp | Numb/swollen feet -> elevate, dry & exit
visual: Time-progression immersion-foot timeline showing wet-cold exposure buildup, daily dry-sock reset, early numbness cues, and stop-travel clinical exit. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Prevent snow blindness (UV photokeratitis) and protect irritated eyes
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Eye Injuries and NPS Mountain Safety; new manuscript

action.text: Wear wrap-around UV-blocking sunglasses or goggles continuously on snow, ice, and open water—even on hazy overcast days, because snow reflects intense ultraviolet radiation upward into unprotected eyes.

Recognize delayed snow-blindness symptoms appearing 4 to 12 hours after exposure: severe gritty burning pain, tearing, swollen lids, headache, and extreme light sensitivity that can leave a traveler temporarily unable to open their eyes.

Move into dim shelter, remove contact lenses gently, rest with eyes closed under a cool clean damp cloth, do NOT rub the eyes, and arrange guided exit and clinical eye evaluation if severe pain or vision loss persists.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Shield corneas from intense snow and water UV glare and manage painful delayed snow blindness safely.
applies: Bright snowfields, frozen lakes, glaciers, high elevations, and overcast bright snow glare.
equipment: Wrap-around UV400 sunglasses or glacier goggles, spare sunglasses or improvised narrow-slit glare shield, and cool clean damp cloth.

failure.text: Hiking across a bright white lake on a cloudy March afternoon without sunglasses because the sun is behind thin clouds.

verify.text: Confirm UV eyewear is worn before stepping onto snow/ice/water and spare eye protection is accessible.

stop.text: Severe light pain, tearing, or impaired vision halts solo or hazardous travel immediately until guided out to safe shelter and medical review.

diagram: Snow/ice reflects UV even in clouds | Wear wrap-around UV400 eye cover | Gritty pain 4–12 h later -> shade, rest & MD
visual: Environmental UV-reflection schematic showing direct plus snow-reflected UV rays reaching unprotected eyes versus wrap-around UV400 shielding. Conceptual, not to scale.

title: Cool and hydrate alert heat-exhaustion patients before heat stroke develops
origin: CDC Heat Health and NIOSH Heat-Related Illnesses; new manuscript

action.text: Stop all exertion immediately at the first heat-exhaustion signs, move the person into shade or air conditioning, loosen heavy clothing/packs, and lay them down slightly elevated feet if dizzy.

Cool actively by applying cool wet cloths or misting cool water over skin while fanning air across the body, and offer small steady sips of cool safe water or labeled oral rehydration solution ONLY while fully alert and not vomiting.
Monitor mental clarity continuously—never leave a heat-exhausted person unattended to "rest in a hot tent," because heat exhaustion can deteriorate silently into fatal heat stroke.

technical_review: AI editorial check; qualified reviewer pending
objective: Halt heat-exhaustion progression rapidly with shade, active cooling, and measured oral hydration while watching for neurological red flags.

title: Activate 911 and begin rapid cooling immediately for suspected heat stroke
origin: CDC NIOSH Heat Illnesses; new manuscript

action.text: Call 911 IMMEDIATELY for suspected heat stroke (altered mental status, slurred speech, collapse, or very high body heat)—remember exertional heat stroke can occur even with heavy sweating and in moderate temperatures during hard effort.

Begin aggressive external cooling IMMEDIATELY while waiting for EMS: immerse the trunk/limbs in cold water if safely available (keeping head and airway strictly supported above water), OR douse continuously with cold water and cold wet towels rotated over neck, armpits, groin, and torso while fanning vigorously.

Do NOT force fluids by mouth into a confused, drowsy, or vomiting patient; follow 911 dispatcher directions continuously and obtain mandatory hospital clinical evaluation even if alertness briefly improves.

title: Manage severe sunburn, solar blistering, and compound heat dehydration

action.text: Move out of direct sun immediately, apply cool damp clean cloths gently to tender skin, wear loose soft sun-blocking fabric over the area, and rehydrate steadily with safe potable water.
Leave intact sunburn blisters unbroken and avoid petroleum jelly, butter, or topical benzocaine/home remedies that trap heat or trigger allergic skin reactions.
Escalate to prompt clinical evaluation for widespread blistering, severe facial swelling, fever, chills, nausea, confusion, or signs of blister infection (pus, spreading red streaks).

title: Halt ascent immediately at early Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS) cues
origin: CDC Travel to High Altitudes; new manuscript

action.text: Suspect Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS) whenever a recently ascended traveler develops headache plus nausea, loss of appetite, unusual fatigue, dizziness, or poor sleep—remembering fitness does NOT protect against altitude illness.
Stop ascending IMMEDIATELY—never climb higher to sleep with AMS symptoms; rest at the current elevation, stay hydrated and warm, avoid alcohol/sedatives, and monitor closely with a companion.
Descend promptly to a lower elevation if symptoms fail to improve after rest or worsen in any way, rather than pushing over a high pass.

objective: Prevent mild altitude headache from progressing into fatal high-altitude lung or brain swelling.

equipment: Elevation map, written symptom tracker, shelter/warmth, safe hydration, and pre-planned lower-elevation descent route.

failure.text: Calling a throbbing high-altitude headache and vomiting "normal trail fatigue" and hiking 2,000 feet higher to camp.

stop.text: Any worsening headache, repeated vomiting, shortness of breath at rest, or stumbling balance transitions immediately to emergency HAPE/HACE descent.

title: Execute assisted descent and rescue for life-threatening HAPE and HACE
origin: CDC Travel to High Altitudes; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize HAPE (shortness of breath while resting, dry or pink frothy cough, chest tightness, extreme fatigue, bluish lips) and HACE (ataxia/staggering walk as if intoxicated, confusion, slurred speech, severe lethargy)—both are rapidly fatal without descent and medical care.

Activate emergency rescue immediately AND organize assisted descent to substantially lower elevation as soon as terrain, weather, and party safety permit—NEVER let an impaired HAPE/HACE patient descend alone or wait until morning if safe assisted descent is feasible.

Keep the patient warm, minimize their physical exertion (carry their pack, support balance closely, or await SAR evacuation if steep/night terrain makes moving unsafe), and leave prescription altitude medications strictly to clinicians or the patient's own prescribed regimen.

title: Assess lightning-strike casualties safely using reverse triage and CPR
origin: NWS Lightning Tips and American Red Cross; new manuscript

action.text: Check immediately whether active lightning still threatens the exact spot—if feasible, move casualties quickly to safer enclosed shelter or lower-risk ground, noting that lightning victims do NOT retain an electrical charge and are completely safe to touch immediately.

Apply lightning "reverse triage" when multiple people are hit: check unresponsive, non-breathing victims FIRST (because lightning frequently causes immediate survivable respiratory/cardiac arrest) while conscious crying/groaning victims are breathing.

Activate 911 immediately, start trained/dispatcher-guided CPR and AED use on anyone not breathing normally, and arrange clinical evaluation for ALL struck persons (checking burns, hearing/eye injury, and spinal precautions).

objective: Provide safe immediate resuscitation after a lightning strike without exposing rescuers to ongoing storm danger.
applies: Outdoor group struck by direct lightning or ground current during a thunderstorm.

failure.text: Avoiding touching a struck teammate out of fear of leftover electricity, or tending a conscious bruised hiker first while a non-breathing victim goes without CPR.

verify.text: Confirm scene safety, immediate 911/CPR for non-breathing victims first, and medical referral for every affected party member.

stop.text: Ongoing close lightning requires moving victims to safer ground rapidly while maintaining continuous CPR and EMS activation.

title: Recognize anaphylaxis and assist with a patient's prescribed epinephrine
origin: NIH MedlinePlus Anaphylaxis; new manuscript

action.text: Recognize anaphylaxis immediately when exposure triggers ANY airway/breathing sign (swollen lips/tongue/throat, hoarseness, wheezing, trouble breathing), dizziness/fainting, widespread hives/flushing, or severe cramps/vomiting.

Call 911 immediately and assist the patient in administering their OWN prescribed epinephrine auto-injector into the outer mid-thigh strictly per the device label (can go through light clothing); log exact injection time.

Do NOT delay epinephrine waiting for oral antihistamines to work, never use someone else's prescription without direct clinician/dispatcher authorization, and keep the patient lying flat (or seated upright if breathing is easier—never suddenly standing).

objective: Spot rapidly fatal multi-system allergic reactions and support timely use of the patient's own prescribed auto-injector plus 911 activation.

equipment: Patient's own prescribed unexpired epinephrine auto-injector (if carried), watch, and 911 communication.

failure.text: Giving an over-the-counter antihistamine and waiting thirty minutes while throat swelling progresses to complete airway closure.

verify.text: Confirm 911 is dispatched, exact auto-injector time is recorded, and breathing/alertness are tracked continuously.

stop.text: If severe symptoms fail to improve or worsen after 5 to 15 minutes and the patient carries a second prescribed dose, follow the device/dispatcher directions and expedite EMS transport.
